title: Doppler shift from a moving source
prior_knowledge_summary: A progressive wave transfers energy without a net transfer of matter.
Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by v=fλ.
From Lesson 8, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
new_learning: Explain how motion of a sound source changes wavefront spacing in front of and behind the source.
Predict whether a stationary observer detects a higher or lower frequency as the source approaches or recedes.
not_yet_taught: Choose the denominator sign or calculate with the moving-source Doppler expression.
Analyse a stationary source with a moving observer.

blocks.heading: Why does the siren slide downward?
content: An ambulance passes a person standing beside the road. Its siren note sounds higher while it approaches and lower after it passes, although the siren itself keeps vibrating at the same frequency. What changed?
The source moved between sending one compression and the next. That motion changes the spacing of the sound wavefronts reaching the stationary listener.

figure.purpose: Create the Doppler puzzle by comparing approach and recession around one stationary observer.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch in three moments: ambulance approaching, level with, then receding from a fixed roadside listener. Use sparse arrows and the words higher note and lower note, but no formula.
figure.alt_text: A stationary listener hears a higher siren note during approach and a lower note during recession.

blocks.heading: The source keeps moving between wavefronts
content: Imagine the source emits one compression, moves forward, then emits the next. In front, the second compression starts closer to the first, so the wavefront spacing is smaller. Behind, the source has moved away from the first compression, so the spacing is larger.
The sound speed in still air is set by the medium. Source motion changes the spacing of successive wavefronts, not the speed at which each wavefront travels through the air.

figure.purpose: Show how successive emission positions create compressed and spread wavefronts.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper top-view sequence with a source at three successive positions. Draw circular wavefronts centred on each earlier position, crowded ahead and spread behind. Mark one fixed observer on each side and one source-motion arrow.
figure.alt_text: Successive wavefronts are closer ahead of a moving source and farther apart behind it.

blocks.heading: Spacing controls arrival rate
content: A stationary observer in front meets the closer wavefronts more often. More wavefronts arrive each second, so the observed frequency is higher than the source frequency.
A stationary observer behind meets the wider-spaced wavefronts less often. Fewer arrive each second, so the observed frequency is lower.
This is the controlled definition: change in observed frequency caused by relative motion between a wave source and an observer.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: change in observed frequency caused by relative motion between a wave source and an observer

figure.purpose: Connect wavefront spacing to arrivals per second and observed frequency.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison. Left lane: close fronts crossing a stationary observer's counting line with many ticks per second. Right lane: wide fronts with fewer ticks. Label higher observed frequency and lower observed frequency.
figure.alt_text: Closer wavefronts arrive more frequently, while wider wavefronts arrive less frequently.

blocks.heading: A train approaches a platform
content: A train horn emits steadily while the train approaches a person standing on a platform. Choose the region between train and person. The source is moving into this region, so successive wavefronts there are closer together.
Their speed through the still air is unchanged. Because their spacing is smaller, they reach the person more often, so the observed frequency is higher than the horn's source frequency.
After the train passes and recedes, the person lies behind the source. The wavefronts reaching the person are farther apart, so the observed frequency is lower.

figure.purpose: Model a complete qualitative approach-to-recession explanation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper paired train-platform sketches. First panel compresses wavefronts between approaching train and fixed person. Second spreads wavefronts between receding train and the same person. Include reasoning arrows spacing to arrival rate to observed frequency.
figure.alt_text: An approaching train produces closer wavefronts and a higher observed frequency; a receding train produces wider wavefronts and a lower observed frequency.

blocks.heading: The sound does not travel faster in front
content: It can feel as if an approaching source pushes the sound forward so that it travels faster. That would explain an earlier arrival, but it does not explain the continuing higher arrival rate correctly.

In still air, every wavefront travels at the same sound speed. The source changes where each new wavefront begins. This changes wavelength and therefore arrival frequency, while wave speed in the medium stays unchanged.
Do not confuse a louder sound with a higher frequency. Intensity and pitch describe different properties.

figure.purpose: Correct the speed and loudness misconceptions without using the Lesson 10 equation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper myth-versus-model panel. Cross out faster wavefront arrows ahead. Show equal-length speed arrows on all fronts, unequal spacing, and a separate small intensity-versus-frequency reminder card.
figure.alt_text: All wavefronts have the same speed in still air, but their spacing differs; intensity is separate from frequency.

blocks.heading: Use the wave equation as a check
content: Suppose sound travels at 340 m s$^{-1}$. Ahead of a moving source, wavefront spacing is 0.68 m. From the earlier wave-equation module, $f=v/\lambda=340/0.68=500$ Hz.
Behind it, spacing is 0.85 m, so $f=340/0.85=400$ Hz. The smaller spacing gives the higher arrival frequency.
This calculation checks the qualitative model. It is not the moving-source Doppler formula, which comes in Lesson 10.

figure.purpose: Reconnect wavefront spacing to the already-taught wave equation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-row worked layout: ahead uses 340 divided by 0.68 equals 500 Hz; behind uses 340 divided by 0.85 equals 400 Hz. Carry units and add a smaller spacing means higher frequency check.
figure.alt_text: At equal wave speed, spacing 0.68 metres gives 500 hertz and spacing 0.85 metres gives 400 hertz.

blocks.heading: A four-link explanation
content: Start with source direction. Decide whether the source moves toward or away from the stationary observer.
Then follow one causal chain: source motion changes wavefront spacing; spacing changes arrivals per second; arrivals per second set observed frequency.
Approach means closer wavefronts and higher observed frequency. Recession means wider wavefronts and lower observed frequency. Keep sound speed in still air unchanged.

figure.purpose: Provide a compact qualitative decision routine for practice.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper branching map beginning source motion. Approach branch: spacing smaller, arrivals more frequent, observed frequency higher. Recession branch: spacing larger, arrivals less frequent, observed frequency lower. Side note: wave speed unchanged.
figure.alt_text: A decision map links source motion to wavefront spacing, arrival rate and observed frequency.

misconceptions_addressed: Sound travels faster ahead of a moving source.
A higher pitch must be caused by greater intensity.
The emitted source frequency changes merely because the source moves.
